The early history of Rome was marked by a series of monarchies, with seven kings ruling the city from its founding until the expulsion of the last king, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, in 509 BC. This event marked the beginning of the Roman Republic, a period characterized by a system of governance in which power was held by the people and their elected representatives, rather than a monarch.

During the Roman Republic, Rome expanded its territories through a series of conquests, including the subjugation of the Italian peninsula and the defeat of rival city-states such as Carthage. The Roman Republic was also marked by a series of internal conflicts, including the struggle between the patrician class, who held power and wealth, and the plebeian class, who were the common people. This struggle, known as the Conflict of the Orders, ultimately led to the establishment of the Twelve Tables, a set of laws that protected the rights of the plebeians and helped to establish the principle of equality under the law.

As the Roman Republic continued to expand, it faced a series of external threats, including the invasion of the Gauls, who were defeated by the Roman general Camillus in 390 BC. The Roman Republic also faced internal challenges, including the rise of powerful generals such as Marius and Sulla, who would eventually play a role in the downfall of the Republic. Despite these challenges, the Roman Republic continued to thrive, and by the 1st century BC, it had become one of the dominant powers in the Mediterranean.
